attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite name and tile in the [place sprite on top of random tile] block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you move the correct blocks into the [on button pressed] container?

❓ What happens when you press the A button? 


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to notice the different frames in the [animate frames] block, and how that makes the cookie sprite appear to be “eaten”. Encourage the ninja to think about how else they might use the animation blocks to customize their projects.
steps.instructions:
Start the project by making the cookies appear on the screen when the A button is pressed! 


Open Controller and drag out an [on button pressed] container. Then, drag the [set sprite to] and [animate frames] blocks from the [on start] container into the [on button pressed] container.


Drag a [place sprite on top of random tile] block into the [on button pressed] container, above the [animate frames] block. Select cookieSprite as the sprite name and the tan background tile. 


Click ▶ to see Food sprites appear on the screen each time the A button is pressed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use milliseconds (ms) to set the lifespan to a random number between 1000 and 3000?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What do 1 and 3 seconds look like as milliseconds?

❓ What else might happen when the cookie sprite is destroyed?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Remind the ninja that they can convert values from seconds to milliseconds by multiplying by 1000. In this case, 1 second is equal to 1000 milliseconds, and 3 seconds is equal to 3000 milliseconds.
steps.instructions:
Code the cookies to disappear from the screen after a random amount of time!


Drag a [set sprite [x]] block into the [on button pressed] container, underneath the [place sprite on top of random tile] block. Select cookieSprite as the sprite name, then select [lifespan] from the dropdown menu.


Drag a (pick random) block into the parameter and update the values so that the cookieSprite is randomly assigned a lifespan between 1 and 3 seconds.


Drag out an [on destroyed] container, update the sprite kind to Food, then drag a [sprite start effect] block into the container. Drag a (sprite) bubble into the sprite name and update the effect and interval parameters to make the cookies disappear in an exciting way.


Click ▶ to see the Food sprites stay on the screen for a random amount of time, then be destroyed by a special effect!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the correct sprite kind in the (array of sprites of kind) value block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when you use a [forever] loop in a project?

❓ What do you think the number of cookies might be used for in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the placement of each block matters. Make sure that they have placed the (array of sprites of kind) value block inside the (length of array) block, inside the parameter of the [set score to] block.
steps.instructions:
Keep count of how many cookies are on the screen!


Drag out a [forever] loop and add a [set score to] block inside. Then, open Arrays and drag a (length of array) block into the parameter of the [set score to] block. 


Open Sprites and drag an (array of sprites of kind) value block into the parameter of the (length of array) block. Delete (list) and update the sprite kind to Food.


Click ▶ to see the number of Food sprites displayed on the screen! See how many cookies can appear at once by pressing the A button as fast as possible!

steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja:

❓ Which comparison symbol represents greater than?

❓ What value should be in the right parameter of the <0=0> comparison block?

❓ What event will cause the game to end in a win?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Encourage the ninja to think through the logic of the [game over] block. In this example, the game will end in win if the length of the Food sprites array (the number of cookies on the screen) is greater than 25.
steps.instructions:
Challenge the player to make 25 cookies appear before the timer runs out! 


Add a [start countdown] block into the [on start] container and update the interval parameter to be short enough so the game is challenging.


Drag an [on countdown end] container onto the editor and place a [game over] block inside. Replace the [game over] toggle with a <0=0> comparison block. 


Duplicate the (length of array) and (array of sprites of kind) blocks from the [set score to] block and place them in the left parameter of the <0=0> comparison block. Update the rest of the <0=0> comparison block so the game ends in a win if more than 25 Food sprites appear on screen. 


Click ▶ to try to make 25 cookies appear on the screen before the timer runs out!

steps.hints: ❓Did you create a createCookie function and define the function with blocks from the [on button pressed] container?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:


Ask the ninja::

❓ Why might it be useful to use a function in a project?

❓ What do you think the createCookie function will be used for?

❓ What happens when you press the A button now? Is the function being used yet?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Guide the ninja through the process of selecting the Functions code block menu and creating a new function. Help them notice the pop up window, type in the name of their function, and then find the new function container on the editor.
steps.instructions:
Code a second button to make it possible to make 25 cookies appear! 


Use a function to make it easier to repeat the code that creates the cookies. Functions are used to repeat a chunk of code multiple times, and will only run when they are called. 


Click Advanced, then open Functions and select [Make a Function...]. This will define the function. In the pop up window, replace “doSomething” with “createCookie”, then click Done. 


Drag all of the code blocks from the [on button pressed] container into the [function createCookie] container that has appeared in the editor.


Click ▶ to notice what happens now, when the A button is pressed.

steps.hints: ❓Did you use a [call createCookie] block in both  [on button pressed] containers?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓How can you create a function call block in a project?

❓ What happens when the A and B buttons are pressed? 

❓ If there is only one block in each of the [on button pressed] containers, why do multiple actions happen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that there are multiple ways to create a function call block in a project. Once a function has been defined, a function call block will appear in the Functions code block menu which can be dragged into the editor. Alternatively, the ninja can right click on the function definition block in the editor, then select “Create ‘call _______” to create the function call block.

💡 Reinforce to the ninja that if they are using and defining a function in a project, nothing new will happen unless they also call the function to run at a particular time.

💡 Remind the ninja that they can use buttons on their keyboard to control the A and B buttons. They can press “Z” or “SPACE” to control the A button, and “X” or “ENTER” to control the B button.
steps.instructions:
Oh no—no cookies appeared on the screen! That’s because a function has to be called to run the code inside the function definition container. 


Click Advanced to open Functions. Drag a [call createCookie] block into the empty [on button pressed] container. 


Create a new event for the B button by dragging out another [on button pressed] container and selecting “B” as the button.


Right click on the [function createCookie] container and select “Create ‘call createCookie’”, then drag the [call createCookie] block into the [on B button pressed] container. 


Click ▶ to see if pressing the A and B buttons makes it easier to make 25 cookies appear on screen!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Customize this project by adding directions with a dialog box.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.introduction: Create a project that uses a function to set and destroy Food sprites, when a certain button is pressed.

validationItems.text: Code the A button to create a Food sprite every time it is pressed.
Use a random number to set the Food sprite’s lifespan, then destroy the sprite with an effect.
Set the score to continuously show the number of Food sprites on screen.
Use a countdown timer that ends the game in a win if there are more than 25 Food sprites on screen.
Define a createCookie function with the Food sprite’s code already in the A button pressed container.
Call the createCookie function when both the A and B button are pressed.
Use a dialog box to provide game instructions.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Orange Belt! Before you create your final Orange Belt project, there are a few neat tricks to learn that could take your game to the next level! In this level, you’ll learn more about functions, which are chunks of code that run whenever they are called. You’ll learn how to create your own functions to simplify code and make something happen multiple times in a project. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: Function Junction
badges.description: Create functions, with and without parameters, to make something happen in a project.

badges.title: Make Your Own Way
badges.description: Create a new function to be used in a project.

badges.title: Don't Forget To Call
badges.description: Call a user-created function in a project.

badges.title: Customize Your Own Way
badges.description: Create a new function that takes a parameter to be used in a project.

badges.title: Area Code
badges.description: Call a user-created function that takes a parameter in a project.
